newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan export, industry figures boost economy hopes.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan export, industry figures boost economy hopes.

text.p: Taiwan's growth in exports and industrial output in March indicate a strengthening economic recovery, but no major rebound is likely until the third quarter, economists said on Tuesday.

"March's strong export orders and industrial output performance support the viewpoint that Taiwan's economic performance would be stable in the first half and sound in the second half," said National Securities economist Lin Kuo-yang.
"But hit by the hog foot-and-mouth disease, Taiwan's economy is not expected to see major recovery until the third quarter," Lin said.

Government agencies had forecast that the hog disease, which broke out in March and resulted in a pork export ban, would reduce the island's gross domestic product growth between 0.39 and 0.50 percentage points in 1997.
The government in February predicted a 1997 GDP growth of 6.28 percent.
Taiwan said last week it had lifted the export ban, but officials said exporters must obtain permits from importing countries in advance.
Exporter orders for Taiwan goods rose 5.61 percent to US$10.473 billion in March compared to March 1996, the economics ministry said on Tuesday.
The total was sharply higher than an average forecast for a slow 1.95 percent growth that resulted from an April 18 Reuters poll of Taiwan economists.
The island's industrial output in March rose 10.01 percent compared to March 1996, the largest increase in two years and far above an average forecast for a 5.57 percent rise in another Reuters poll.
For the first three months in 1997, export orders showed a 2.12 percent year-on-year growth, while industrial output rose 5.74 percent.

The economics ministry attributed the rise to companies rushing to make up for lost production following a new national holiday in February which reduced the number of working days that month to only 17.5.

"The high growth is somewhat misleading due to the extra February holiday this year," the ministry's chief statistician Chang Yao-chung told reporters. "The first three months' figures should be looked upon as a whole for a more accurate reading."
"But the high growth does indicate a stable recovery in the economy," he said.
Taiwan's star high-tech industries, including information, telecommunications and electronics sectors, contributed most to the two figures' high growth, economists said.
In the March industrial output, information electronics index surged 19.39 percent year-on-year.
In the export orders, information and telecommunications gained 14.72 percent from a year ago.
"The strong growth of the electronics and information industries should largely ease worries over a slow export growth," said Lin of National.
But HSBC James Capel economist Stephen Wang was more conservative.
"The strong performance of the information and electronics industries is mainly due to their product price rebounds, and other industries did not show apparent recovery," Wang said.
"So, whether the electronics industry can continue its sound performance and whether the overall economic recovery can turn stronger in the coming months remain to be seen," he said.
